preamble: Depalatalization (hardening) of [bʲ] to plain [b] removes the palatal secondary articulation. In Slavic it is especially visible with word-final soft labials: Proto-Slavic *golǫbь 'pigeon' and *drobь kept soft [bʲ] in Russian (голубь [ˈɡoɫʊpʲ], gen. голубя) but hardened in Ukrainian, Belarusian, Czech, Slovak and Bulgarian, where the inflected forms show plain [b] throughout the paradigm.

examples.note: Ukrainian has no final devoicing, so the hardened [b] surfaces directly; contrast Russian голубь [ˈɡoɫʊpʲ], gen. голубя, which keeps the soft labial.
The hard-stem genitive дробу shows plain [b]; Russian дробь [dropʲ], gen. дро́би, keeps the soft labial.
The final labial hardened (and is devoiced word-finally); the genitive го́луба shows plain [b].
Czech lost the palatalized labials altogether; the genitive holuba shows plain /b/ (the nominative is devoiced word-finally). Slovak holub [ˈɦɔlup], gen. holuba, is parallel.
The definite forms гълъбът and гълъба show a hard [b] before the back-vowel article.

sources: Shevelov, G. Y. (1979). A Historical Phonology of the Ukrainian Language. Carl Winter. https://lccn.loc.gov/80494566
